526.title: Ashtpadi 23, salok: the ointment of wisdom
526.hook: giaan anjan gur deeaa: the Guru gave the ointment of wisdom and the darkness went (Sukhmani 23)
526.howItsDone: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib's twenty-third ashtpadi begin with a salok picturing the Guru's wisdom as anjan, eye-ointment, that ends the darkness of ignorance.

segments.voice: Yesterday, living ashtpadi 22, and your line: everything alive is his. Did something neglected get a moment of care? Today the twenty-third ashtpadi begins, and it starts with the eyes. Day five hundred twenty-six.

In many Punjabi homes, there's a small bottle or a little metal pot of surma, a fine dark powder for the eyes. A grandmother might line a baby's eyes with it, or her own, with a thin stick, an old custom across South Asia. People say it cools the eyes and protects them. Gurbani's word for eye-ointment like this is anjan. And the twenty-third ashtpadi of Sukhmani opens with the Guru putting anjan on someone's eyes.
screen: `A LITTLE POT OF SURMA.` → `LINED WITH A THIN STICK.` → `ANJAN, FROM THE GURU.`

segments.voice: The salok, in paraphrase: the Guru gave the ointment of spiritual wisdom, and the darkness of ignorance was destroyed. By God's grace I met the holy one, and Nanak's mind was lit up. Take it in pieces. Giaan is wisdom, knowledge, especially the kind that knows God. Anjan is the eye-ointment, the kohl or surma. So giaan anjan is wisdom pictured as a balm for the eyes. And notice who applies it: the Guru, gur deeaa, the Guru gave it. You don't put it on yourself. Then the result: agiaan andher binaas. Agiaan is the opposite of giaan, not-knowing. Andher is darkness. Binaas means destroyed, gone. The darkness isn't argued away; it simply ends, the way a dark room ends when someone opens the shutters. The second line adds how it happened: har kirpaa, by God's grace, the seeker met the holy one. And the last word is pargaas: light, illumination, the mind lit from within. Look at what ointment actually does. Ointment doesn't add anything new to the world. The trees, the faces, the sky were all there already. It just lets you see them. That's how Sikh teaching often talks about the Guru's wisdom: not as information piled on top of life, but as clearer eyes for the life that's already in front of you. Over the next days, the twenty-third ashtpadi will show what those cleared eyes see.
screen: `GIAAN ANJAN: WISDOM AS EYE-BALM.` · `GUR DEEAA: THE GURU APPLIES IT.` · `THE DARKNESS ENDS, LIKE SHUTTERS OPENING.` · `NOT NEW THINGS: CLEARER EYES.` · then, large: `THE GURU CLEARED MY EYES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: wash your eyes with cool water. If you can, go to a sink. Cup cool water in your hands and bring it gently to your closed eyes, two or three times. Dry them slowly. Then sit, eyes closed, and feel the coolness fade. When you're ready, open them slowly, and let the first thing you see simply be there. If you pray, you can say Waheguru as you open your eyes. The bell holds the time.
Ashtpadi 23. Its salok: the Guru gave giaan anjan, the eye-ointment of wisdom, and the darkness of ignorance was gone.
Your line: the guru cleared my eyes. Today, before you judge a situation, take one breath and look at it again, as if with cleared eyes. Day five hundred twenty-six.

527.title: Seeing Him everywhere
527.hook: with cleared eyes, He is seen within and without (Sukhmani 23)
527.howItsDone: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib's twenty-third ashtpadi hear that God is seen within, in the company of the holy, and then in all things; Guru Tegh Bahadur's hymn teaches knowing the One within and without.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ashtpadi 23, and your line: the guru cleared my eyes. Did you look twice at something before judging it? The ointment is on. Today we find out what the cleared eyes see. Day five hundred twenty-seven.

You can lose your glasses while wearing them. It's a classic: patting every pocket, checking under the couch cushions, asking the whole house, until someone points at your face. The thing you were searching for was right there, closer than anything else, which is exactly why you couldn't find it. Gurbani makes a similar point, in earnest. The twenty-third ashtpadi says the One we go searching for is seen, by cleared eyes, both within and without.
screen: `LOOKING FOR THE GLASSES YOU'RE WEARING.` → `CLOSER THAN ANYTHING.` → `WITHIN AND WITHOUT.`

segments.voice: The first stanza after the salok begins, in paraphrase: in the company of the holy, I saw God within. God's Name began to taste sweet. All things are held within the One, appearing in many colors. Antar is within, inside, the inner self. The cleared eyes look in first, and find God there, antar prabh deethaa, God seen inside. But the stanza doesn't stop at the inner room. It turns outward, to all things and their many colors, all held in the One. Guru Tegh Bahadur, the ninth Guru, puts the two directions side by side in a hymn in raag Dhanasari. In paraphrase: why go searching in the forest? God lives in everything, yet stays untouched, and is with you too. Like fragrance in a flower, like a reflection in a mirror, God dwells within; search in your own heart. Within and without, know the One. That, he says, is the wisdom the Guru gave. Notice the two pictures. You can't see the fragrance in the flower, but it's all through it. You can't pull the reflection out of the mirror, but it's really there. That's how the Gurus speak about God within. And the forest matters too. The hymn speaks to seekers who leave home for the forest to find God, and its answer is gentle: you don't have to go anywhere. Look in, then look around. The same One is in both places.
screen: `ANTAR: GOD SEEN INSIDE.` · `THEN OUTWARD: MANY COLORS, ONE.` · `FRAGRANCE IN A FLOWER, A FACE IN A MIRROR.` · `NO NEED FOR THE FOREST.` · then, large: `WITHIN AND WITHOUT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look within, then around. For the first minute, close your eyes and look inward. Notice the breath, the heartbeat, the quiet under the thoughts. Don't hunt for anything; just rest there. Then, slowly, open your eyes and look around the room or out the window, with the same quiet attention. Let the inside and the outside sit together. If you pray, you can say Waheguru once inward, once outward. The bell holds the time.
Seeing Him everywhere. Cleared eyes find God antar, within, and then in all things outside; Guru Tegh Bahadur says: within and without, know the One.
Your line: within and without. Today, each time you step outside, take one breath inward first, then one look around. Day five hundred twenty-seven.

528.title: The seer and the seen
528.hook: He is both the one who sees and what is seen (Sukhmani 23)
528.howItsDone: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib's twenty-third ashtpadi hear that God is both the one who sees and what is seen, and teachers explain this both as oneness and as presence within a God who is also beyond.

segments.voice: Yesterday, seeing Him everywhere, and your line: within and without. Did you take a breath inward and a look around? Today the twenty-third ashtpadi turns the question around: not what the eyes see, but who is seeing. Day five hundred twenty-eight.

Point your phone's camera at a mirror. On the screen you'll see the phone, and in the phone's screen a smaller phone, and inside that a smaller one, shrinking off into the distance. The camera is looking at itself looking. It's a fun trick for about ten seconds, and then it gets a little dizzying. Who's the watcher here, and what's being watched? Sukhmani's twenty-third ashtpadi gives a startling answer to that kind of question. God is both. The seer and the seen.
screen: `A CAMERA FACING A MIRROR.` → `LOOKING AT ITSELF LOOKING.` → `THE SEER AND THE SEEN.`

segments.voice: The twenty-third ashtpadi, having cleared the eyes and shown God within and without, takes one more step. In paraphrase: God Himself is the one who sees, and God Himself is what is seen. Gurbani uses this pattern of aap, Himself, often: God Himself the speaker and the listener, the giver and the receiver. In Japji, Guru Nanak says that the Creator, having made the world, watches over it. Sukhmani goes a step further. The watching itself, the light in your eyes, comes from God. Here's one way to feel it. Every time you look at something, there are two ends: you, looking, and the thing you look at. Usually we only notice the thing: the tree, the screen, the face. We almost never notice the looking. Sukhmani says both ends are held by the One. In that picture, the tree is God's play, and the light by which you see the tree, the jot within, is God's Light too. Drisat is the word for sight or glance. Now, Sikh teachers explain this in more than one way, and it's fair to say so. Some stress oneness: there is finally only God, seeing God. Others stress that God is present in all, and yet beyond all, so the creature and the Creator stay distinct even while the Light is shared. Gurbani holds the mystery without settling it in a slogan. Either way, the practical turn is the same. In Sukhmani's picture, seeing is not a small, private thing; it's lit by the One.
screen: `AAP: HIMSELF, AT BOTH ENDS.` · `THE TWO ENDS OF EVERY LOOK.` · `THE LIGHT YOU SEE BY IS HIS.` · `TEACHERS READ IT MORE THAN ONE WAY.` · then, large: `THE SEER AND THE SEEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: watch yourself watching. Pick one thing to look at: a cup, a window, your hand. Look at it for a few breaths. Then, without looking away, notice the looking itself: that you're aware, that light is reaching you, that something in you is seeing. Rest in both at once, the thing and the seeing. If your mind wanders, come back to the cup. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru as the light you see by. The bell holds the time.
The seer and the seen. Sukhmani says God is at both ends of every look: the light that sees, and the world that is seen.
screen: `THE SEER AND THE SEEN — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the seer and the seen. Today, three times, stop and notice not just what you're looking at, but that you are looking. Day five hundred twenty-eight.

529.title: Living ashtpadi 23
529.hook: clear sight is a gift, not a skill
529.howItsDone: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib's twenty-third ashtpadi hear that clear sight comes by God's grace and the Guru's wisdom, and they keep daily practice as a way of making room for that light.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the seer and the seen, and your line was the same. Did you catch yourself looking, three times? Today we carry the whole twenty-third ashtpadi, the cleared eyes, out into the day. Day five hundred twenty-nine.

The first week in a new apartment, you notice everything. The way the light hits the kitchen at four o'clock. The creak in the third stair. The neighbor's wind chime. A year later, you walk past all of it without a glance. Nothing changed. The light still comes in at four. You just stopped seeing it. That fading is ordinary, and easy to miss. The twenty-third ashtpadi has something to say about it, from an unexpected direction.
screen: `THE FIRST WEEK: YOU NOTICE EVERYTHING.` → `A YEAR LATER: NOTHING.` → `AN UNEXPECTED ANSWER.`

segments.voice: Here's the twenty-third ashtpadi in brief. The Guru applies giaan anjan, the eye-ointment of wisdom, and the darkness of not-knowing ends. With cleared eyes, God is seen within and without. And God is found at both ends of every look, the seer and the seen. Now, the natural modern response to all that would be: great, how do I train my eyes? What's the technique? Sukhmani gently sets that aside. Look again at the salok. Who gave the ointment? The Guru. How did the seeker meet the holy one? Har kirpaa te: by God's grace. Clear sight, in this ashtpadi, isn't a skill you master like a language or a golf swing. It's a gift you receive. That doesn't make practice pointless. Sikh practice still includes amrit vela, the company of the sangat, recitation. One way to picture it: practice is more like opening the shutters than building a lamp. In the salok's picture, the light comes from elsewhere. You can make room for it; you can't manufacture it. And there's real freedom in that. If seeing freshly were a skill, every dull, blurry day would be your failure. If it's a gift, then a blurry day is just a day the shutters stuck, and tomorrow the light may come in again. The last word of the salok is pargaas, the mind lit up. Not lit by effort; lit, the way a room is lit when the sun comes through.
screen: `THE ASHTPADI: OINTMENT, SIGHT, SEER.` · `HAR KIRPAA TE: BY GOD'S GRACE.` · `OPENING SHUTTERS, NOT BUILDING LAMPS.` · `A BLURRY DAY IS NOT A FAILURE.` · then, large: `SEE FRESHLY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pause and see freshly. Choose something you see every day and never notice: a doorframe, a mug, the view from your usual chair. Look at it as if you'd just moved in. Its color, its shape, a scratch, the way light lands on it. Don't force a feeling. Just leave the shutters open and see what comes in. If nothing does, that's fine too. If you pray, you can say Waheguru as you look. The bell holds the time.
Living ashtpadi 23. Clear sight comes by grace, har kirpaa te; practice opens the shutters, and pargaas, the light, comes in.
Your line: see freshly. Today, on your most familiar route, look up once and find one thing you've never noticed before. Day five hundred twenty-nine.

screen: `DAY 529 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: ASHTPADI 24, SALOK: THE PERFECT LORD.`

pairs: the shutters stuck, not a failure

530.title: Ashtpadi 24, salok: the perfect Lord
530.hook: pooraa prabh aaraadhiaa: I worshiped the perfect Lord (Sukhmani 24)
530.howItsDone: Sikhs reciting the final ashtpadi of Sukhmani Sahib begin with a salok that names God pooraa, perfect and whole, four times, moving from worship to finding to song.

segments.voice: Yesterday, living ashtpadi 23, and your line: see freshly. Did you spot something new on a familiar route? Today Sukhmani reaches its last ashtpadi, the twenty-fourth. Day five hundred thirty.

Listen to how often you say perfect in a day. The barista asks if oat milk is okay: perfect. A coworker says the meeting moved to three: perfect. Your friend says she's running ten minutes late: perfect. We've worn the word down until it means fine, or got it, or sure. Sukhmani's twenty-fourth ashtpadi opens with that same word, pooraa, four times in two short lines. And it means it, every time.
screen: `OAT MILK? PERFECT.` → `A WORD WORN DOWN TO FINE.` → `POORAA, FOUR TIMES.`

segments.voice: The salok, in paraphrase: I worshiped the perfect Lord, whose Name is perfect. Nanak has found the perfect One; sing the praises of the perfect One. Pooraa means full, complete, whole, lacking nothing. A pooraa glass is filled to the top. A pooraa job is finished. When Gurbani calls God pooraa, it means nothing in God is missing or partial, and nothing needs to be added. Count the word as it goes: the perfect Lord, the perfect Name, the perfect One found, the perfect One praised. It's like a bell rung four times. And look at the order. First, aaraadhiaa: I worshiped, I remembered with devotion. Then paaiaa: I found, I attained. Then the invitation: gaau, sing. Worship leads to finding; finding spills over into song. That's the whole of Sukhmani in miniature. It's fitting that this is the last salok. Over twenty-three ashtpadis, Sukhmani has walked through nearly everything a life holds: pride and humility, slander and praise, wealth that stays behind, the wanderer at the door, the stillness before creation, the eye-ointment of wisdom. Now, at the end, it gathers all of that into one word. Not a summary of the argument, a word of praise. After all the teaching, what's left here is gratitude, sung. The word we've worn down to fine gets its weight back here. Full, whole, lacking nothing. In these two short lines, only one thing is called that, four times running.
screen: `POORAA: FULL, WHOLE, LACKING NOTHING.` · `FOUR TIMES, LIKE A BELL.` · `WORSHIP, THEN FINDING, THEN SONG.` · `THE LAST SALOK GATHERS IT ALL.` · then, large: `THE PERFECT ONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: praise once. Sit quietly and let one thing come to mind that's full and good: a person's kindness, a view, a piece of music, the fact of your own breathing. Stay with it until gratitude rises on its own. Then let it out once, in a single word or phrase, quietly or aloud. If you pray, the word can be Waheguru, which itself is a word of wonder and praise. Then rest in the quiet after it. The bell holds the time.
Ashtpadi 24. Its salok rings pooraa four times: the perfect Lord, the perfect Name, the perfect One found, the perfect One praised.
Your line: the perfect one. Today, each time you say perfect out of habit, let it remind you of the One the salok means. Day five hundred thirty.

sources.ref: Sukhmani Sahib, ashtpadi 24, salok (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 295)

531.title: Perfect is His way
531.hook: perfect is His way and perfect His Word (Sukhmani 24)
531.howItsDone: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib's last ashtpadi hear of the perfect Guru, Word and way, and meet hard days with bhaanaa, acceptance of God's will, remembering God with each breath.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ashtpadi 24, and your line: the perfect one. Did a habitual perfect remind you of anything? The salok rang pooraa four times. Today: what does a perfect way look like on a day that isn't? Day five hundred thirty-one.

The car won't start. The rain comes in sideways. The email you were waiting for says no. By ten in the morning the day is clearly not going to be a perfect one, and the whole thing starts tilting. Then Sukhmani's last ashtpadi says something that sounds almost cheeky on a day like that: perfect is His way, and perfect His Word. It isn't saying the car will start. It's saying something about what lies underneath the day that won't.
screen: `THE CAR WON'T START.` → `THE EMAIL SAYS NO.` → `PERFECT, UNDERNEATH?`

segments.voice: The twenty-fourth ashtpadi keeps ringing the word pooraa, perfect, through its stanzas. Its first stanza begins, in paraphrase: listen to the teaching of the perfect Guru; see the Supreme as near you; remember God with every breath, and the anxiety of the mind will lift. Perfect Guru, perfect Word, perfect way. Now, here's what perfect is not claiming. It isn't claiming that every day will feel perfect, or that bad things don't happen. Sikh history has martyrdoms in it, Gurus among them. The tradition doesn't pretend life is smooth. What it claims is something underneath the surface of the day: that God's hukam, God's order, is whole, even when we only see a ragged piece of it. Sikhs speak of meeting the day that way as bhaanaa mannanaa: accepting bhaanaa, God's will. Guru Arjan, who wrote Sukhmani, sings in another hymn, in paraphrase: whatever You do seems sweet to me. Sikh tradition remembers that he lived those words to the end. That's the kind of trust this stanza points to. Not pretending the rain isn't sideways. Trusting there's a whole beneath the part. And notice the practical line in the middle: remember God with every breath, and the anxiety lifts. Saas saas. The trust isn't a big leap made once. It's breath by breath, on the imperfect day itself. Perfect, underneath; imperfect, on top. Sukhmani asks the reciter to live in both.
screen: `THE PERFECT GURU, THE PERFECT WORD.` · `NOT A CLAIM THAT DAYS FEEL PERFECT.` · `BHAANAA: GOD'S WILL, ACCEPTED.` · `SAAS SAAS: BREATH BY BREATH.` · then, large: `PERFECT, UNDERNEATH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: trust one imperfect day. Bring to mind what's gone wrong today, or this week. Name it plainly to yourself. Don't argue with it. Then, on each breath in, hold the thought: this is the surface. On each breath out: there's a whole underneath. Breath by breath, like the stanza says. You don't have to feel the trust. Just practice it. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath. The bell holds the time.
Perfect is His way. Sukhmani says God's order and Word are whole even when our day isn't; Sikhs meet it with bhaanaa, trust in God's will, breath by breath.
Your line: perfect, underneath. Today, when something goes wrong, take one slow breath before reacting, and say the line silently. Day five hundred thirty-one.

532.title: The ambrosial Name
532.hook: sukhmanee sukh amrit prabh naam: this jewel of peace is the ambrosial Name (Sukhmani 24)
532.howItsDone: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib pause at its rahao line, which calls the jewel of peace God's ambrosial Name, resting in the minds of devotees.

segments.voice: Yesterday, perfect is his way, and your line: perfect, underneath. A week ends today. The Guru cleared the eyes; we saw within and without, the seer and the seen, learned to see freshly, then met the perfect One. Today, the line the whole bani is named for. Day five hundred thirty-two.

Plenty of books take their title from one line buried inside them. You're reading along, and there on an ordinary page is the phrase from the cover, and suddenly the whole book makes a little more sense. Sukhmani has a line like that. It isn't saved for the end. It's planted near the very beginning, and the bani's name comes from it. As Sukhmani closes, we turn back to it: the ambrosial Name.
screen: `A TITLE ON AN ORDINARY PAGE.` → `PLANTED NEAR THE BEGINNING.` → `THE AMBROSIAL NAME.`

segments.voice: The line comes right after Sukhmani's first stanza, marked rahao, which means pause: the place in a hymn where you stop and take in the center. In paraphrase: Sukhmani, the jewel of peace, is the ambrosial Name of God; it rests in the minds of the devotees. Start with the name of the bani. Sukh is peace, ease, happiness. Mani can be read as a jewel, so Sukhmani is often called the jewel of peace; some also hear man, the mind, in it, peace of mind. Either way, the line tells you what that jewel actually is. It isn't the poem. It's the Name. Then amrit. Amrit is the nectar of immortality in old Indian stories, the drink of the gods. In Gurbani, amrit comes up again and again: the amrit vela before dawn, the amrit of the Name, and the amrit Sikhs receive at initiation. It means what gives true life, sweet and undying. And the last phrase: bhagat janaa kai man bisraam. Bisraam is rest, a place to stop and lay down a load, like a traveler's inn. The Name is where the devotee's mind comes to rest. One way to read Sukhmani, then: all twenty-four ashtpadis, with their warnings and their stories, their stillness and their praise, unpack this one line. Pride and humility, wealth and kindness, the wanderer and the beggar, the cleared eyes: each was a way into the same rest. Sukhmani's peace is not a mood. It's a Name, remembered.
screen: `RAHAO: THE PAUSE AT THE CENTER.` · `SUKHMANI: THE JEWEL OF PEACE.` · `AMRIT: WHAT GIVES TRUE LIFE.` · `BISRAAM: WHERE THE MIND RESTS.` · then, large: `THE NAME IS PEACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rest in peace for one minute, and then a second. Sit comfortably and let the body grow heavy. With each breath, imagine setting down a load, the way a traveler sets down a bag at an inn. One load per breath: a worry, a task, a conversation. If you pray, you can let the Name, Waheguru, be the place where you set each one down. If you don't, let the breath itself be the resting place. The bell holds the time.
The ambrosial Name. Sukhmani's rahao line says the jewel of peace is God's amrit Name, the place where the devotee's mind finds bisraam, rest.
Your line: the name is peace. Today, at one stressful moment, pause and set down one load on a single breath. Day five hundred thirty-two.
